patches.old: (the median white family holds approximately **7–8 times** the wealth of the median Black family in the U.S.)
patches.new: (in the Federal Reserve's 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, the median white family held about **six times** the wealth of the median Black family — roughly $285,000 against $45,000 — and about five times that of the median Hispanic family; the ratio narrowed slightly from 2019 while the dollar gap widened)

patches.old: women earn approximately **82 cents** for every dollar earned by men (overall median), with gaps widening at higher income levels and in certain occupational sectors.
patches.new: the size of the gap depends on which workers are counted, so note the measure before comparing figures. On the most recent Census data, women working **full time, year round** earned about **84 cents** for every dollar earned by men, while across **all workers** — including part-time and part-year — women earned about **78 cents**. The gap is consistently wider for Black and Hispanic women measured against white men, and it widens at higher income levels and in certain occupational sectors.

sources.title: Federal Reserve, “Greater Wealth, Greater Uncertainty: Changes in Racial Inequality in the Survey of Consumer Finances” (2023) — the typical white family had about six times the wealth of the typical Black family in the 2022 SCF
Center for American Progress analysis of Census Bureau annual income data — women working full time, year round earned 84 cents per dollar earned by men, and 78 cents across all workers

visual.title: The types, the two measures, and the matrix
visual.alt: A grid crossing intergenerational against intragenerational mobility with upward and downward examples in each cell and a note that horizontal mobility involves no change of stratum; a panel contrasting absolute mobility, with the 90 per cent of the 1940 cohort and about 50 per cent of the 1984 cohort who out-earned their parents, against relative mobility; a transition row comparing a perfectly mobile 20 per cent in each quintile with the observed distribution for children born in the bottom fifth; and a panel of the IGE, rank-rank slope, Gini coefficient and Great Gatsby curve with their values.
visual.caption: A country can have plenty of absolute mobility and almost no relative mobility — everyone richer, the same families on top.
